[PAPER_0034, relevance_score=0.310] In both studies, we expected that all respectively examined state and trait empathy components are positively associated with everyday IER goals and hedonic IER goals. Regarding counter-hedonic IER goals, we expected that all empathy components, except personal distress, show positive associations with counter-hedonic IER goals.

[PAPER_0036, relevance_score=0.288] As prior lab and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies have shown that empathic processes can be moderated by how close regulators feel to their targets (e.g., Beeney et al., 2011; Rauers et al., 2013), all our analyses controlled for feelings of relationship closeness to the regulatees.

We did not preregister prior hypotheses for associations between empathy and IER goal attainment, as the primary outcome of this investigation was IER goal setting.

[PAPER_0037, relevance_score=0.252] Based on the scarce evidence for a positive association between empathy and IER goal attainment, we expected a positive relationship between all empathy components and goal attainment.

We used an EMA paradigm to address these aims and investigate these hypotheses. EMA provides the opportunity to capture empathy and regulatory behavior with a high ecological validity by measuring social interactions in people's natural environments.
items.paper_content_summary: The paper predicts positive associations of all empathy components with general and hedonic IER goals. [PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.472] Study 2

Method

Participants

All procedures were approved by the IRB at Yale University (New Haven, Connecticut, United States). The recruitment process was identical to Study 1, except that we also used ResearchMatch, a national health volunteer registry created by several academic institutions and supported by the U.S. National Institutes of Health. ResearchMatch has a large population of volunteers who have consented to be contacted by researchers about health studies. Moreover, we distributed flyers in the New Haven, Connecticut, area.

[PAPER_0044, relevance_score=0.400] [From Study 1, cited for: Recruitment through online ads, with ResearchMatch additionally used] One hundred thirty-five participants with a mean age of 25.50 years (SD = 7.96 years, range = 18-59 years) self-identified via online ads that invited adults between the ages of 18 and 65 years to participate in an online EMA study about others' emotions.

[PAPER_0051, relevance_score=0.426] Procedure

The overall study procedure was consistent with Study 1. The only modification was that we increased the study duration from 7 to 10 days. All data were collected between March 14, 2022 and June 23, 2022.

[From Study 1, cited for: Overall study procedure, with duration increased from 7 to 10 days] Ads contained a link to a study description and informed consent form.

[PAPER_0155, relevance_score=0.413] Fourth, although we endeavored to increase the generalizability of our findings by recruiting a community sample for Study 2 and using samples from Germany and the United States, we would like to note some constraints on the generality of our findings. For instance, although our sample in Study 2 is significantly more gender-balanced, our results may be affected by gender differences in empathy (e.g., see Clarke et al., 2016).

[PAPER_0080, relevance_score=0.368] Results

We excluded 23 participants who completed only one EMA survey and 260 incomplete EMA surveys due to missing data in the IER goals variable. Another 89 single surveys were excluded due to their large RSI values (Leiner, 2019b). Subsequently, we excluded 16 participants who had zero variance across their empathy ratings. In the final step, we removed six participants with only one EMA entry left after these exclusions.

[PAPER_0081, relevance_score=0.347] This resulted in a final sample of 204 participants (82.93% of the original sample) with a mean age of 30.06 years (SD = 7.35, range = 18-60) who reported a total of 3,992 social interactions. Of these, n = 142 participants completed at least 50% of the EMA entries. Results of the entire sample were identical to results for participants with at least 50% compliance; analyses retaining the full sample are presented. Further information on the final sample can be found in Table 1.
